Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

review_text_raw:
Review originally posted [url=https://www.backlog-assassins.net/posts/z7q2vd7/]here[/url].

9/10

This was a hell of a game. It’s one of an emerging genre of… ‘interface’ games, I guess. Like Her Story, you are literally your character in the game - what you see on screen is what your character sees, and you interact in the same way. Because of this, the game is incredibly immersive and therefore, at points, really tense!

Let me stop myself before I get too deep in here. In Orwell, you play as, ostensibly, yourself, hired as an ‘investigator’ in this new program called Orwell situated in a different country. In that country, a bomb has just exploded in a plaza, killing two and wounding a dozen or so people. Moments before the bomb went off, a woman was spotted crossing the plaza and getting on a bus. That woman had been arrested months before for assaulting a police officer in that very same plaza during a protest. Could she be connected to the bomb? Your task is to slowly collect information on her, and the people around her. What information you upload to the system cannot be taken back, and you get to choose what the narrative of what happened becomes. You can take an innocuous joke between friends and upload it, taking it out of a friendly context and giving it a sinister cast. You can shift a bias on a person by only uploading the worst of what they said, but not uploading good things about them. In this story, YOU are the faceless watcher, the cog in the wheel, that would be impeding the heroes of a more traditional story.

Holy shit, does it work.

I blasted through the game’s five chapters in one sitting, about four and a half hours on Saturday night. Nobody in this game is 100% good or bad, and there’s a lot of nuance around protesting for the ‘right’ reason in the ‘right’ way that is especially topical for me, right now, as a young woman living in an America I never really thought I’d be living in. This game doesn’t deliver any hard and fast morals at the end, it doesn’t take a definitive stance, and offers three different endings for the player to eventually pick. The game offers up a scenario and leaves it up to you to decide what you think is right… or at least, what you think is the least wrong.

The game isn’t perfect - it wears a little thin when you’re going back and achievement gathering. Like a Telltale game, once you see the constraints of the ‘world’ of the game, the illusion dissipates pretty quickly. There are a lot of real-time sections (text conversations, phone calls) that, while immersive the first time around, made me really wish I had a fast forward button for the fourth or fifth time I sat through the conversation. These are absolutely small gripes, however, and I would strongly urge anyone to pick up this game - especially while it’s still on sale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

11/10 would hack the local fishing society again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is simple:
It's a game where you play a investigator who works for the government, sifting through data in all of its forms in order to fight for the safety of the public in the fictional world that it's set in.

There have been many 'hacking' games that have come out over the years, but Orwell takes the idea and puts you in the position of 'good' rather than 'bad', which creates the core ideology of the game -- If what you're doing is so good, then why do you feel so bad doing it?

The game proceeds along a UI of sorts, one that allows you to sift through websites, personal pages and even listen on some incredibly well-simulated 'real time chats', along with interruptions and intentional spelling errors that betray the typer's emotions and mental states. It's one of the best simulations of texting I've seen before in a game, and it DOES stand out. The articles and websites, while simple and clean, are detailed and packed full of worldbuilding -- the developers go out of their way to fill the world with detail that was never necessary to get from point A to B, but still fill everything with life and activity, and the world ends up feeling a little bit less compartmentalized than other games which force you into a limited POV.

However, this all leads back to the internal condundrum I have with this game:
You work with a handler who analyses the information you send him, and it's his job to make sense of it all. All you do is forward him the pertinent information, enough for him to make decisions and calls on how to handle situations. And you must choose what it is you want to send.

It's your choice to pick A over B. And it's not outright lies, because you're the good guy, remember? But whatever you send can tinge a thought, affect outcomes and colour perceptions in slight, yet pertinent, ways. Your own analysis plays a big part in how you want to portray someone else, and ultimately, the only one who has to live with the decisions you make is yourself.

Orwell is a great game about people, but more than that, it's a platform to help you examine yourself as a person. Since you're doing this for the percieved good, what decisions will you make and how far will you go to get what you want? And is there ever a time when personal freedom can be infringed upon for the greater result? Well... that might be another question for another time.

It's a good game tho, eh?

(( P.S.: Like any other 'visual novel' style game, and including the horrendous works of Mr. David Cage, I am fully aware that some of these 'choices' may be nothing more than illusionary. However, the game does it well enough in its context that reflecting upon the choices you make actually makes more than just a surface-level difference since you're playing not a character, but yourself. And considering the game's name and influences, I believe this to be the point. ))

The reason this review is "Positive" is that there's not "Meh" button, and I don't want to hate on things for no reason, either.

The message is pretty much predictable, and while you might have certain doubts/hopes in the beginning that there will be arguments for both sides - spoilers - well, there are none.

UI is a little clunky, the characters are mostly annoying stereotypical millenials, and, frankly, fuck me for spending 5 hours on it, I do have - simply more fun - things to do in my life. But, funnily enough, I felt compelled to finish it, so then again, maybe it's not so bad?..

I guess it has something to do with a Bad TV Show syndrome - it's mediocre, but once you're in, there's an itch inside to see the story through. The story is meh-ish, and kind of weird: the 'big' plot twist is...well...real bad, i'll just leave it at that, while there's a certain number of small unexpected things that are implemented...just really well, as in you don't see them coming, and in the same time they fit the story really well.

That all said, I have no idea why there's a season 2, except for the dev wanting more monies, especially having seen the ending(s) and all.
Is there something wrong with it? - No.
Will I be playing season 2? - oh fuck no.

4.5-5/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Interactive story hidden behind a simple detective game [/h1]

While the game's premise sounds pretty interesting, the gameplay is quite simple. You read various things such as Internet pages (forums, bank account extract, company's webpage, etc), chat discussions,  listen to live calls which are transcribed and some parts of the text will be highlighted which you can then drag and drop to [b]Orwell[/b], a database which unlocks additional things if a link can be established with the information you've taken.
For a non-spoiler example: you search a person's personal blog and you can find and analyze their username which can then be linked to another forum where it's used for more juicy contents.

It's a bit like [u]A Lost Phone[/u] but its puzzles are MUCH simpler and you can't really get stuck for too long as there's plenty of helpful indicators. Actually, the best part of the game where I really concentrated was when the amount of datachunks (highlighted parts of data in texts) you could import was limited. This really made you think if a [strike]favorite color[/strike] hobby such as artist is a valuable piece of data or not (you could be redirected to an artist page showing past gigs/locations or a contact phone number!).

The best part of the game is the story, because in the end, there's a story and it's told little by little, there are some interesting plot parts (Sorry won't spoil anything) and even if the gameplay sounds boring, the pace is really good and I didn't see time pass by while I finished the 5 episodes. It takes a little bit more than one hour per episode, maybe faster if you just drag and drop without reading.
Even if having a [i]know it all[/i] tool, there are plenty of mysteries to uncover and discovering bit by bit the personalities and relationships of the people you [strike]spy on[/strike] is pretty addictive.

The presentation is pretty nice with its stylish interface. Graphics isn't the most important part of the game but it's good that it's pleasing to the eyes. The music does also its job, it changes when there's a [b]gasp[/b] moment. 

In summary, I recommend this game if you like simple but well told story in a different way than just watching Netflix. It has a nice conspiracy/detective vibe and getting to the finish is an entertaining (and bumpy) ride.
I have definitely put the season 2 on my wishlist!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A very interesting narrative experience that pulls you in quite well with busywork, much like Papers, Please. It has a very well-crafted and smooth user interface that could totally pass for a real spying program. The game gives you loads of freedom in how you selectively pass on information to alter the plot, and everything from what you choose to save to WHEN you choose to save it can affect the course of the story. At times, these flashpoints are signposted a little too hard, presumably to give players plenty of time to sort through the information at hand and come to a decision, but there are multiple instances when you have to make genunely DIFFICULT choices relying only on your intuition and the information you have gathered thus far. The game does not hold your hand about the consequences your actions will have.

However, the ending did feel a bit contrived and (while foreshadowed well enough), not terribly well justified. I know too well the amount of work that must have gone into such an involved branching story, but the game felt too short. Just when it was beginning to get difficult and the amount of information you had to deal with started to grow burdensome, the game ends. It feels a bit rushed out the door, and doesn't give you enough of a chance to play with the mechanics and start to really sweat. Ultimately, this reveals the underlying issue with Orwell: It is not a game. It is a moral lesson wrapped in an interactive experience. The developers had something they wanted to say, and so the game must come to an end so that they can say it.

I completed the 5-day story in 3-4 hours, but it has some replayability in going back to explore alternate outcomes if you had taken different paths. However, this robs the game of its magic; because you're making difficult decisions based on limited info, a blind playthrough adds a considerable amount. On your second playthrough, you're really just going through the motions to see what happens, which makes the leisurely pace at which characters interact torturous and tends to expose the man behind the curtain when you see how your choices DON'T affect the story.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Guys!  Perhaps this may come as a shock to some of you but, in case you didn’t know, this game has a bit of an agenda….[/b] 
Ok ok, joking aside I bought Orwell a while back when it fell below my “if I buy this and don’t like it, I won’t feel any great loss” threshold.  It sat in my library untouched until a rainy day when I didn’t feel like getting into anything too involved.  I say this to admit that I went into this with pretty bland expectations.  

I generally view games like this the way I do a book from an unknown author, but that has a premise I like.  I knew going in that the game makers had a point to make and even though it was a point I generally agree with, I was a little wary.  [i]I don’t like being preached at, so I wasn’t sure if I was going to spend the entire game being beat over the head with the rhetoric bat whilst being presented with billboards saying in big bold letters “Hey look, the authors feel very strongly about this” at every turn or if the game would have any merit beyond the political statement.[/i]  [b]I’m very thankful to say that this game was far more than just a tray upon which to serve political and social commentary and it was even very clever in doing so.[/b]

So why did I start out with all that waffle about political commentary?  Because I want to set the tone for how I approached the game and the preconceptions I had going in.  I went into the experience thinking that I pretty much had them figured out and that I would easily be able to see through any “hard choices with lasting consequences” to what the authors were really trying to sell to the player.  And chapter 1 pretty much was just that.  I “knew” they were trying to get me to suspect a particular person and that they wanted me to assume the simple answer so they could jump out from behind the posterized, low-polygon trees and say “Ha!  See how even with all the information at your fingertips you jumped to the wrong conclusion.”  So naturally I did just the opposite.  Purposefully ignoring what I assumed were red-herrings and by the end of chapter 1, I’d almost lost interest figuring that I had it all figured out.  I was delighted, and a bit disappointed, that I was wrong.  

Starting chapter 2, I was actually engaged in the narrative and was now determined not to be caught off-guard again.  I still knew there was a point to it all, but I wasn’t as sure I knew what that point was.  By the end of the game, I knew what was going on, but because I’d fed information to orwell earlier on that seemed harmless at the time, I’d built a profile on some of the characters that was not incorrect but was misrepresentative.  This led to events playing out in a way that I didn’t want and with no way to go back and correct.  I felt duped, but in a good way.  The game had indeed gotten it’s point across, but in a very subtle and engaging way that left me still feeling that I enjoyed the experience.

So let’s sum this up, shall we? 
•	Orwell was well worth the money
•	Gameplay was not nearly as on-rails as I had expected
•	Story was actually very engaging and believable
•	Plot twists did not feel super-contrived simply to force the player to be wrong for the sake of proving a point.  All the plot twists could have been seen coming I think if the user had paid attention to the details and not just focused on what Orwell highlights.
•	The game actually made me think and didn’t preach it’s point smugly from contrived moral high-ground and I appreciated that.  

Here is where I would usually list a few things that could have been improved, but the game is pretty simple and the UI layout is simple and easy to use.  Some of the “websites” that you visit have clickable links that aren’t obvious… that was kind of annoying, but not too bad.  I’d like to say that I wish you could go back and edit information when you found out it was wrong, but I think it’s integral to the game the concept that YOU are the filter.  If it’s not relevant, accurate, or then you don’t upload it.  If I had one complaint it would be that I sometimes didn’t know what would “trigger” the next event and so sometimes I’d upload something I didn’t really want to just because I thought I had to in order to progress the game.   

All in all, the game took me about 6 hours to play through… you could go longer or shorter, but in the end, it’s not a great investment timewise…. In fact, it practically gives you a good stopping point between chapters.  I highly recommend the game.  It’s worth $7-10 for your time and as a good conversation starter.  Gift it to a friend so you can have a good conversation on the topic.  

Anyway, That’s my 2 cents worth.

-John

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Smart, subtle, and shockingly good: this one lingers long after the credits.[/h1]

Ever wondered what it would feel like to be Big Brother’s favorite intern? Orwell hands you the surveillance keys to a digital dystopia and asks: how far is too far when safety is on the line? Presented through simulated internet searches, social media sleuthing, and a stripped-down but powerful interface, this game is one of the most immersive narrative experiences I’ve played!

The choices are yours: what do you report? What gets ignored? You might think you're just dragging datachunks into files, but your decisions have real consequences, shaping a gripping narrative with multiple endings and gray-area morality at every turn. It’s as if Papers Please had a love child with 1984 and that baby learned to code.

There is a catch though : this isn't really a “puzzle” game despite the label (it’s more like an interactive spy-thriller/visual novel hybrid with branching paths and big philosophical questions). That said, I devoured it across three playthroughs to 100% the game and would gladly do more. Whether you’re a dystopia enthusiast or just looking for a smart, haunting slow burn, Orwell belongs on your must-play list, especially when it goes on sale (but even at full price, it’s a steal with around 4 hours of game play per playthrough).

P.-S. Stop reading about this masterpiece and go play it yourself. You'll thank me later for stopping you from reading too much. Going in blind is the best way to enjoy it!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is loosely based on the concept of mass surveillance depicted by Orwell in 1984. While it can't be compared to the depth and complexities of the novel, it does the job of provoking thought with sleek user interface, eye catching graphics and well written articles and dialogues. But the decision on whether the public safety and national security could justify the blatant invasion of privacy is yours to make. Did the Orwell system serve it purposes in your hand and protect national secuirty and innocent citizes, or was that a blatant abuse of authority which will ultimately imprison the freedom of thought? With all the information that you stole and acquired through questionable means, did you even catch the right culprit? It's good to ponder whether you did the right thing at the end of the game there, sometimes.
One thing though, the letters can be a bit too small or too light colored for such a text intensive game like this, there should be an option for text sizes or color.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a very interesting game, especially for anyone who has an interest in the surveillance state and the pros and cons of such a thing, mixed in with choices that really seem to matter.  I will admit that I have have, at the time of writing this review only played one playthrough, but the story was compelling and the information that I chose to put in/leave out really seemed to impact what was happening.  On top of that, the story is compelling, interesting and told through a very interesting way, feeding you snippets as you dig through the personal lives and media presence of several NPCs with various connections to one another, with a simple lock-off system that makes sense in-universe (we don't have clearance to investigate this person who has some connection to a potential suspect).

Beyond that, the only real issue I have with the game is the few interface bugs.  As the game went on, I found myself getting glitched to certain websites, mostly the [spoiler]work profile of the concerned one woman after she died in a shootout with law enforcement, and occasionally it would glitch to her dating profile.  This would normally happen when I was in either the listener or insider tools, seemingly never when I was on the reader tool already.  It would just switch me over as I tried to open a file on the insider, or load up into a machine, or even when I'd try opening a new conversation in the listener.[/spoiler]
One more slight drawback about the game is that sometimes you get told a bit too much by the game.  Game not letting you progress?  Something you thought was a lie was probably true.  Yellow highlight instead of blue?  You're going to get some information that conflicts with that.  I realise it would be a lot more work but a way to mark information as lies rather than just disabling it might help.  People don't always tell the truth and if you come to the conclusion that something true is a lie, it would be nice if the game didn't give away that you're wrong by just stopping time for you.  As for the other issue, it might be nice getting a window saying "Hey, this piece of information you're trying to add conflicts with this other information you've already added...which one do you think is true?", instead of just "Hey, at some point probably in the next 10 minutes you'll get another piece of information that will conflict with this here, we know that even though in-universe we haven't made the connection that that page with the conflicting information even exists!"

All in all a really great game with a simple premise, easy to learn with some fairly minor flaws that can honestly be overlooked most of the time.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is an entertaining game that clearly draws inspiration from a literary classic "1984" and delivers a profound message regarding the dangers of excessive surveillance and the delicate balance between privacy and security. As a player you take on the role of a Big Brother investigator in the dystopian world of The Nation, employing Orwell, an information gathering and surveillance software to spy on people. By sifting through relevant or conflicting text messages, emails, calls and posts, you dive into the intricate web of communication to uncover the culprits behind various crimes. Every datachunk you choose to upload to Orwell has consequences.

The game's minimalist interface, immersive gameplay and intriguing storyline are highly enjoyable, but there are certain areas that could certainly be improved: the tedious and non-skippable dialogues, somewhat abrupt endings and limited control over the game's progression.

The story is very rich, well plotted and flows through lots of twists and turns. The gameplay itself is not that challenging (only thing that might have needed a bit more) but the story will keep you hooked. There's and ironic twist on how things turn out (not sure how close to the end I've reached) that [spoiler] gives some sort of satisfaction seeing a specific person tasting his own poison. [/spoiler]

The interface and gameplay is straightforward with no issues whatsoever. The game is polished with attractive stylized graphics. The narrative is well written.

I loved the game concept and really enjoyed playing the game. I should be right around the corner to find out what happens at the end, unless another plot twist takes this a bit further.

A 100% Recommendation
